newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia agrees debt deal with Lon club--officials.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia agrees debt deal with Lon club--officials.

text.p: Bosnia and the London Club of creditors clinched a debt agreement in time for a deadline expiring on Monday night, Western officials said on Tuesday.
"We do have an agreement," a U.S. official mediating the talks between Bosnian representatives and commercial creditors told Reuters.
The debt agreement had looked uncertain on Monday evening when Bosnia's Serb entity raised last-minute objections, financial officials said.
Negotiations began last Wednesday with commercial bankers from the London Club to restructure Bosnia's $1.04 billion debt.
Under the agreement, Bosnia assumes responsibility to service $404 million of the $1.04 billion sum.
Bosnia, devastated by a 43-month war of independence, will pay $105 million at low interest rates over an extended period.
In the first five years, interest rates will be set at two percent and rise to three percent in the following two years.
From the seventh to the tenth year, the rate will rise to 3.5 percent. After ten years, the rate will be based on Libor (London Inter Bank Offered Rate) plus 0.825 percent.
The remaining $254 million would not be paid until the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita rises to $2,800, indexed to German inflation from 1997.
An earlier proposal had set a lower GDP level of $2,500.
As part of the restructuring of the debt, Bosnia would issue bonds denominated in German marks listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange.
The terms meant creditors had agreed to a generous debt reduction of 87.5 percent, officials said. Many creditors had already written off Bosnia's debt due to the war.
After the old Yugoslav federation disintegrated in a bloody war that began in 1991, former republics have had to negotiate their share of a huge debt left over.
The London club issued a one year waiver in June 1996 which required Bosnia to reach an agreement by midnight (2200 GMT) on Monday.

If the deadline had expired without a deal, Bosnia would have faced much more difficult conditions. Their former wartime foes in Serbia and Montenegro -- now known as Yugoslavia -- would have been allowed to enter the negotiations.
Yugoslavia has bought a major stake in the debt and could have blocked any future deal with the London club, foreign experts said.
Former Yugoslavia owed a total of $4.3 billion to the club and since 1992, Serbia and Montenegro have been buying the debt at ten cents to the dollar, acquiring a 38.2 percent stake.

The agreement reached on Monday should help Bosnia restore its relations with financial institutions and to raise funds in international financial markets for peacetime reconstruction, said a statement issued by the signatories.
The Bosnian delegation was led by Moslem co-prime minister Haris Silajdzic and his Serb counterpart, Boro Bosic. Chase Manhattan bank was the chair of the creditors' committee.
